demand_source.supports: Google ships a chat assistant for children under 13 that a parent switches on through Family Link, says it can give clues and explanations so a child works out schoolwork for themselves, and tells parents to explore it with the child and supervise; opened in this run.

edits.description: Later, each child texts Happy from their own Apple account and gets a helper with no tools and no memory, on a local model, that gives grade-level hints and short explanations and is told not to hand over a finished worksheet; the parents get chat hours per child, a text when a message is flagged for safety or distress (meant to arrive at once; how the plugin sends it is not settled), and an evening digest of what each child asked, delivered only by a route that keeps the child's words off the cloud model (still to be checked). Whether a child may chat with Happy alone, or only with a parent alongside, is a decision to take before building. As a second step the same kids agent answers by voice through the roadmap's kitchen speaker (Home Assistant Voice Preview Edition), with wake word, speech-to-text and text-to-speech running locally so that only text reaches Happy.
caveats: Blocked until a local model and local classifiers exist and the kid-safety evals pass, because kids' content never goes to a cloud model or cloud speech.

A local classifier's accuracy on how 8 and 10-year-olds actually write is unproven: false alarms will annoy, misses matter more, and a home system has no human reviewer between the flag and the parent notice.

Common Sense Media rated Google's supervised assistant for under-13s high risk and recommends that children aged 6 to 12 use chatbots only under adult supervision; an alert and an evening digest are a look afterwards, not supervision, so whether a child may chat alone is a decision to take before building.
'Refuse whole-worksheet answers' is a prompt rule, and no source shows a model holds to it when a child pushes.
The alert is a heads-up to parents and not a crisis service, and the parents should be told so.

The speaker has no interim adult version: nothing identifies who is speaking, so without a local model a child's question would reach OpenAI as text, and speech stays in the house only while Home Assistant's own cloud speech option is left off.

The hop from Home Assistant to Happy is unsolved: Home Assistant's official OpenAI integration only talks to OpenAI's own endpoint, and with token auth OpenClaw's chat endpoint gives the caller the full operator scope set and lets the request choose the agent, so the bridge would be a community integration or a self-written kids-only shim.

The speaker adds an always-on VM to patch and back up, Home Assistant itself calls the device a preview, and open-ended questions need Whisper, which Home Assistant recommends only on powerful hardware.
How the safety plugin texts the parents from inside a hook is not settled: no plugin-side send path was found in the hook docs read, so an 'immediate' alert is the aim, not a tested behaviour.

OpenClaw's local-model guide says local models do not come with the hosted providers' safety filters. Keeping the children's chat off the cloud therefore also gives up the vendor's own content filtering, and the local classifier becomes the only filter between the model and a child, which is one more reason the kid-safety evals have to pass first.

demand_source.title: Standing orders (OpenClaw docs)
demand_source.supports: OpenClaw's own guide describes giving each recurring program a written scope, trigger, approval gate and escalation rule in AGENTS.md, run on a schedule by automations.

caveats: A charter is prompt text, not enforcement; the hard limits stay in tool policy and hooks.

AGENTS.md shares a bootstrap budget (20,000 characters per file by default); keep each program to about ten lines. Scheduled runs do not get MEMORY.md, so anything a program needs must be in AGENTS.md, the job message or a tool result.
A chat instruction does not change a charter; it waits for a reviewed deploy.
By default a failure alert goes to the failing job's own announce target, so Jordan would get 'job failed' texts for her jobs unless they are rerouted to Tony.
Alerts start after 2 failures in a row with a 1-hour cooldown. A recurring job is switched off after 10 failures in a row and then disappears from the default job list.
Without a per-job timeout an isolated agent job is bounded only by a 60-minute watchdog.
After a reboot with FileVault locked nothing fires and nothing alerts. One-shot reminders still catch up after an outage even with skipMissedJobs set.

Jobs an agent creates in chat, once

-main holds the automations tool, are outside the registry, so the diff must tolerate or report them.

With triggers on, trigger scripts and script payloads run with the owning agent's full tool policy, exec included. Switching triggers off does not touch the catalog's no-model jobs: the watchers (F018) and the fixed reminders in CRT-04 are command jobs, which OpenClaw's docs list as a separate kind of job from the script payloads, condition triggers and stream schedules that the switch turns off.

Failure alerts cover failed deliveries as well as failed runs, and a failed delivery can alert at once, without waiting for two in a row. OpenClaw's job guide says a text that a plugin hook cancels is recorded as a delivery error, unlike a job that answers the silent token, so the texts the notification policy (G001) or the stop (G005) drop on purpose would reach Tony as failure alerts unless the registry marks those jobs for it. How to do that (best-effort delivery on those jobs is one candidate) is not worked out or tested.

challenge_note: Verdict and the first reviewer's caveat fix upheld (payloads.md lists command and script payloads separately); added a caveat from docs/automation/cron-jobs/managing-jobs.md:159 and delivery.md:127 that a hook-cancelled text is a delivery error that can alert at once.

demand_source.title: Operator incident response: contain (OpenClaw docs)
demand_source.supports: OpenClaw's incident guide makes stopping the Gateway and freezing who may message it the first containment steps, which this card puts one text away for either parent.

caveats: The phrase matcher is a claim hook and message_sending is a delivery hook: both log and continue when their handler throws or times out, so the stop must not live only there.
Command jobs make no agent run, so their announce texts can only be caught by message_sending (as read from the bundled code, not yet tested); the dependable stop for those is the scheduler switch.
/stop (OCL-06) ends one answer in one chat; this stops everything.
For a stolen phone, 'stop everything' already works as the blunt version; the lock-out phrase only keeps Happy answering the other parent in the meantime.
A locked phone already stops most misuse. The lock-out covers a phone taken while unlocked or a passcode seen over a shoulder.
Either adult can lock the other out, and Tony undoes it at the Mac. If whoever holds the phone sends the phrase first, the real owner needs the CLI.
A lock-out stops replies and texts to that person, not their scheduled jobs; pause those too with the mute and vacation controls in G001.
Keep both phrases out of Happy's own help text and replies.

The fixed emergency reply (CRT-13) is planned as a second phrase list in this same plugin. It must keep answering while Happy is stopped or a person is locked out, so whatever cancels outgoing texts during a stop or a lock-out has to let that one fixed line through.

A stop does not stop the scheduler, so its failure handling keeps running underneath. OpenClaw records a scheduled text that a hook cancels as a delivery error, and a scheduled run the stop blocks may count as a failed run (not tested). Tony then gets the registry's failure alerts (G003), which is a useful signal, but a recurring job that fails ten times in a row is switched off and stays off after the stop is lifted, until he re-enables it. For a stop that lasts longer than a day or two, switch the scheduler off as well, and after lifting a stop check the full job list for jobs that were switched off.

demand_source.title: Model failover: user-visible fallback notices (OpenClaw docs)
demand_source.supports: OpenClaw tells the person in a direct chat when another model has answered in place of the usual one and when the usual one is back, once per change, the same down-and-back pair of notices this card sends for an outage.

caveats: OpenClaw's prompt-injection guidance says not to use smaller or cheaper model tiers for agents that have tools or read outside content, and each parent's main agent does both (reminders, lists, family delivery, photos and PDFs). The fallback here is the vendor's lower-cost model, so allowing it is a decision and not a default; without it an outage means the plain notice and no answers until the usual model is back.

OpenAI's status history listed 39 incidents in September 2026 and 23 in the first ten days of October across all its products. Most do not touch the API models Happy uses, but some did, for example 'elevated error rates across API models' on 17 Sep.
An answer from the smaller model can be worse than the usual one; the fallback notice tells the parent which model answered.
No fallback to a second vendor: it would need another vendor's key and a new privacy decision, and the local route is the skipped M2, so a vendor-wide outage still means no answers until it ends.
An API key that hits its monthly cap looks like an outage until the month ends; the fixed line should say 'limit reached' when that is the cause.
If the Mac, the home internet or iMessage is what failed, nothing here helps. The dead-man alert is then the only signal and it goes to Tony.

A scheduled brief that fails is simply missed unless the job's retry settings say otherwise. OpenClaw's scheduler already sends a failure notice after two failures in a row and one recovery notice afterwards, but the jobs registry (G003) routes those to Tony, so the line built here is the only word the family gets.

A parent who texts during an outage is not met with silence today: the failover page says that when every model fails the failure is shown, and that the reply can be a more specific line, such as one saying all models are temporarily rate-limited, with the time the cooldown ends when that is known. What this card adds is the unprompted line to both parents and the 'back' line.

The outage line is an unprompted text and the card set no hours for it: an incident at 03:00 should not text both parents. The host script that sends the line checks the hours itself, and skips the pair altogether when the incident is over before the allowed hours begin. It cannot lean on the notification policy (G001) for this: that card is wave B and this one is wave A, and if the line goes out as a command job, a text that G001's hook cancels is recorded by the scheduler as a failed delivery, which alerts Tony, and not as a quiet drop. Once G001 exists the script reads the same allowed hours from it.

demand_source.title: OpenClaw AGENTS.md template: be proactive
demand_source.supports: OpenClaw's own agent template tells a proactive agent to stay quiet at night and when nothing is new, and lets only an urgent item through.

caveats: Each iPhone can already silence the night on a schedule, so what Happy adds is the daily cap, the urgent or not-urgent split, the label and the pause by chat.

The delivery hook can only rewrite or cancel a text, so one stopped by the daily cap or by quiet hours is dropped, not delivered later; holding texts and releasing them in a batch would need a queue of the plugin's own, which is not designed. Scheduled jobs are therefore timed inside the allowed hours, and the hook is the backstop.

It is not a hard gate for scheduled texts: the message_sending hook that sees `--announce` deliveries lets the message through if the plugin throws or times out, and only the agent's own message tool is gated fail-closed.
The reading of the announce path comes from bundled JavaScript and not a doc page, so confirm it with a throwaway hook before relying on either hook.
No doc lists a job id on message_sending, so each job may have to write its own tag into the text.
No built-in quiet hours or priority classes were found in OpenClaw, so keeping urgent alerts on during a mute depends on this plugin.
The household store does not exist yet, so the counters and the paused-until row are a design and not an installed feature.
The fixed emergency reply (CRT-13) answers an inbound text and must never be held back by quiet hours, caps or a mute.

Timed reminders run with an empty tool list (F007), so a reminder job cannot check the pause itself; its text is stopped only by the delivery hook, which is the best-effort side. A mute is therefore dependable only for jobs that hold the household-store tool and read the row themselves, and best effort for reminders. Because a stopped text is dropped and not sent late, a one-off reminder that falls inside a mute would be lost, so one-off reminders a parent set belong in a class that passes; a recurring one such as the bins reminder can pause, because the next one comes round anyway.

Switching a job off by chat is open only to a command owner, which is Tony's handle alone today (adding Jordan is the open decision recorded on F007). OpenClaw's page gives that sender's agent the power to update, run or remove any job on the Gateway, not only to pause one, and a job changed that way no longer matches the registry (G003). The paused-until row is the route both parents use, and it changes no job.

The evening brief (F014) is specified with the weather and calendar tools only, so as written it cannot read the paused-until row. Give that job the household-store read as well, or its pause rests on the best-effort delivery hook, like a timed reminder's.

A scheduled text that the delivery hook cancels is not a quiet drop on the scheduler's side. OpenClaw's job guide says a job that answers the silent token is recorded as intended silence, with no failure alert, while a text a hook cancels is recorded as a delivery error; a failed delivery can raise a failure alert at once, and the jobs registry (G003) sends those to Tony. So each job whose text the cap, the hours or a mute stops at delivery would show as failed and could alert Tony (once per job while it keeps happening), and the guide implies a one-off reminder stopped this way stays in the job list instead of being removed. This is one more reason to have a job check the pause itself and answer the silent token wherever it can; for jobs that cannot, the registry needs a way to keep intended drops from alerting (best-effort delivery is one candidate). Read from the docs and the bundled code, not tested on this install.

demand_source.title: Fambot: AI Family Assistant (App Store listing by Fambot Inc)
demand_source.supports: A shipping family assistant sells the same function: it reads school emails and newsletters and sends parents a daily digest of what to know, do and decide; opened in this run.

caveats: Pick the mailbox provider with the password in mind: the plugin signs in with a mailbox password only, which on Gmail means a Google app password that Google does not recommend, while OpenClaw's guide names Fastmail and iCloud.

Each school system has to accept an extra guardian address, a manual chore per system. By default the mail plugin lets in only mail that passes its own sender-authentication check, so mail auto-forwarded from a parent's Gmail, or sent by a small club or PTA domain that has not set that up, may be rejected. Registering the address directly is the safe route; for a listed sender whose mail cannot pass the check, OpenClaw's mail guide gives a per-sender address token (a plus-address with a long random token, registered with that sender as the address to write to), which lets that one sender's mail in without the check and does not widen the sender list. The token address is given to that sender only, because mail sent to it under that sender's address is no longer checked for authenticity. Tony sets it up; it is a loosening he owns.
The reader gets body text and attachment file names only, so PDF or image newsletters and flyer attachments are not read.

Urgent alerts are not this digest's job, since the school's own alerts reach the parents' phones first; the reader keeps one backup rule (a closure, delay or early-dismissal message from an allowlisted school sender is passed on at the next sweep, not held until 16:00), and sorting urgent from routine on real district mail is untested.

PowerSchool emails carry grades and attendance and Classroom summaries carry assignment titles: these are a child's education records and they reach the cloud model under store:false, which is why the card is rated medium risk.
Classroom summaries (missing and upcoming work, no grades) arrive only if the school uses Classroom and the teacher switches them on, and the guardian invitation expires after 120 days.
One job appears to take one delivery target, so two parents need two jobs or the parents' group chat, and the iCloud read path likely needs an in-house himalaya wrapper.

For a school or team app that sends no email, try the app's own email notifications into this mailbox first and a parent's screenshot to Happy second; Canvas and ClassDojo have no verified email path.

The reminder step is not wired end to end. The reader that writes the digest holds no reminder or store tool, on purpose, because it reads untrusted mail, and it is untested whether the parent's own agent, which receives any reply, can see the digest text. Until that is tested, a parent names the line when asking their own agent for a reminder. Giving the reader a write to the household store would let text from a school email reach the parents' private agents, so that route needs its own review first.

The sender list lives in family.json5 and changes only with a reviewed deploy, so a parent who needs a new coach or teacher added asks Tony. The mail plugin logs a rejected message without its subject or body, so a mail that did not show up can be traced in the gateway log.
A calendar link that a school platform offers is subscribed in the family calendar (F009), not read by this reader.

The sender check with verified authentication runs only on the mail plugin's per-message path. The 16:00 digest job reads the mailbox itself through the read-only mail tool, so mail from a sender who is not on the list (spam, a faked address) would reach the reader unless the job filters by sender or the digest is built only from what the plugin let in. The reader holds nothing but the mailbox read and can only text the two parents, which limits the harm to a misleading digest line. Which of the two routes builds the digest is not settled. One more fact for that choice: the plugin's path rejects mail whose mailbox date is more than 48 hours old, so a digest built only from what the plugin let in would skip mail that arrived while the Mac was off for more than two days; and OpenClaw's mail guide says a model failure after a message has been let in does not make the plugin read that message again, so mail that arrived during a model outage (CRT-04) would be missing from such a digest too. Both points weigh for the 16:00 job reading the mailbox itself, at the cost of doing without the plugin's authentication check on that path.
